gloss_terse: A clay jar or pitcher used for carrying water, storing flour, or holding other provisions.
gloss_readable: Refers to a common earthenware vessel central to everyday domestic life in ancient Israel. Most memorably, Rebekah carries her kad on her shoulder at the well when Abraham's servant encounters her (Gen 24:14-46), and this same vessel sustains the widow of Zarephath whose flour jar never runs empty during the famine (1 Kgs 17:12-16). In Gideon's night raid, empty jars conceal torches that blaze forth when shattered (Judg 7:16-20). Ecclesiastes uses the image of a pitcher broken at the spring as a poignant metaphor for death (Eccl 12:6). Across languages the translations converge on a medium-sized portable vessel: Spanish 'cantaro/tinaja,' French 'cruche,' German 'Krug.'

senses.1: A medium-sized clay container designed for carrying or storing liquids and dry goods. Evidence from Rebekah's well scene (Gen 24) shows it balanced on a woman's shoulder for water transport, while the widow's jar in 1 Kings 17 holds flour. Gideon's warriors use empty jars to conceal torches (Judg 7:16). Multilingual glosses consistently render it as a portable earthenware vessel (Spanish 'cantaro,' French 'cruche,' German 'Krug'), confirming its everyday domestic character.

gloss_terse: Libnah: a Canaanite city in the Judean Shephelah; also a wilderness encampment on Israel's exodus route.
gloss_readable: Designates two distinct locations in the biblical narrative. The primary Libnah is a fortified city in the southwestern lowlands of Judah, captured during Joshua's southern campaign (Josh 10:29-39) and later assigned as a Levitical city (Josh 21:13). It reappears in the monarchic period as the birthplace of Hamutal, mother of Kings Jehoahaz and Zedekiah (2 Kgs 23:31; 24:18), and as a site besieged by Sennacherib (2 Kgs 19:8). A second Libnah marks a wilderness station between Rimmon-perez and Rissah during the exodus wanderings (Num 33:20-21). The name likely derives from the root lbn meaning 'white,' perhaps referring to the local limestone. The Septuagint renders it as Lebna.

senses.1: A Canaanite city in the Shephelah of Judah conquered by Joshua (Josh 10:29-39), assigned as a Levitical city (Josh 21:13), and historically significant through the monarchy as both a hometown of royal mothers and a target of Assyrian campaigns (2 Kgs 19:8). Also serves as a wilderness encampment name (Num 33:20-21). The name probably reflects the white limestone terrain; the Septuagint consistently renders it Lebna/Lemona.

gloss_terse: Michal: the younger daughter of King Saul and first wife of David.
gloss_readable: A personal name borne by King Saul's younger daughter, who loved David and became his wife (1 Sam 18:20, 27-28). Michal famously helped David escape Saul's assassins by lowering him through a window and placing a household idol in his bed (1 Sam 19:11-17). After Saul gave her to Palti ben Laish (1 Sam 25:44), David later demanded her return as a condition of alliance with Abner (2 Sam 3:13-14). The name is likely a contracted form of Michael, meaning 'Who is like God?' Her story ends in estrangement after she despised David's dancing before the ark (2 Sam 6:16-23). The Septuagint renders the name as Melchol.

senses.1: The proper feminine name of Saul's younger daughter who married David out of genuine love (1 Sam 18:20). She functions as a pivotal figure in the David-Saul conflict, aiding David's escape (1 Sam 19:11-13) and later becoming a political pawn (1 Sam 25:44; 2 Sam 3:13-14). Her final scene, despising David's ecstatic worship before the ark (2 Sam 6:16-23), closes her narrative arc with ironic distance. Multilingual glosses uniformly transliterate the name: Spanish 'Mical,' French 'Mical,' German 'Michal.'

gloss_terse: Manoah: the father of Samson, from the tribe of Dan.
gloss_readable: A proper masculine name meaning 'rest' or 'resting place,' derived from the root nuach. Manoah was a Danite from the town of Zorah whose wife received the angelic announcement of Samson's birth (Judg 13:2-22). He is portrayed as a devout but cautious man who prays to see the angel again and offers a sacrifice on which the angel ascends in the flame (Judg 13:19-20). His alarmed reaction, 'We shall surely die, for we have seen God,' is gently corrected by his more perceptive wife (Judg 13:22-23). Samson is buried in his father's tomb between Zorah and Eshtaol (Judg 16:31). The Septuagint renders his name as Manoe.

senses.1: The personal name of Samson's father, a Danite from Zorah whose narrative fills Judges 13 and closes in 16:31. His name, from the root nuach ('to rest'), ironically contrasts with the turbulence of his son's life. He is depicted as pious and anxious, offering sacrifice and fearing death after the theophany (Judg 13:19-22). Multilingual glosses consistently transliterate: Spanish 'Manoa/Manoaj,' French 'Manoach,' German 'Manoach.'

gloss_terse: Foolish, morally senseless; a person blind to ethical and divine claims, acting with shameful impiety.
gloss_readable: Describes not mere intellectual limitation but a deep moral and spiritual insensibility, someone who fails to perceive God's claims and acts with disgraceful presumption. Moses rebukes Israel as a 'foolish and unwise people' who have forgotten their Redeemer (Deut 32:6), while the psalmist appeals to God against a nabal nation that blasphemes his name (Ps 74:18). When used as a noun, it denotes a person whose folly is willful and culpable, as when Abigail admits her husband's character matches his name (1 Sam 25:25). David's lament asks how Abner could have died 'as a fool dies' (2 Sam 3:33). Job's wife is rebuked for speaking 'as one of the foolish women' (Job 2:10). Isaiah contrasts the nabal with the noble (Isa 32:5-6). Spanish 'necio' and German 'Narr' both capture the moral weight of this term.

senses.1: A person characterized by willful moral and spiritual blindness rather than mere ignorance. The term carries connotations of shameful impiety and base presumption. In Deuteronomy 32:6 it describes Israel's ingratitude toward God; in Psalm 74:18 it labels those who blaspheme the divine name. Used substantively for the culpably foolish person (2 Sam 3:33; Isa 32:5-6; Job 2:10), it stands in sharp contrast to the wise and noble. Multilingual evidence confirms the moral weight: Spanish 'necio,' German 'Narr,' and English 'fool' all carry ethical rather than purely intellectual connotations.

gloss_terse: Nahor: the name of two patriarchal figures, Abraham's grandfather and brother.
gloss_readable: A proper masculine name of uncertain etymology, borne by two important figures in Israel's ancestry. The first Nahor is Abraham's grandfather, the son of Serug and father of Terah (Gen 11:22-25; 1 Chr 1:26). The second and more prominent Nahor is Abraham's brother, also a son of Terah, who married Milcah and fathered Bethuel, grandfather of Rebekah and Laban (Gen 22:20-23; 24:15, 24, 47). The 'city of Nahor' where Abraham's servant finds Rebekah (Gen 24:10) likely refers to a settlement in upper Mesopotamia associated with this family line. In the covenant between Jacob and Laban, both invoke 'the God of Nahor' alongside 'the God of Abraham' (Gen 31:53). The Septuagint consistently renders the name as Nachor.

senses.1: Proper noun identifying two figures in the patriarchal genealogy: (1) Abraham's grandfather, son of Serug (Gen 11:22-25; 1 Chr 1:26), and (2) Abraham's brother, son of Terah, whose descendants include Rebekah and Laban (Gen 22:20-23; 24:15, 47). The 'city of Nahor' (Gen 24:10) locates the family in upper Mesopotamia. Notably, Laban invokes 'the God of Nahor' as a distinct ancestral deity in the Mizpah covenant (Gen 31:53). Multilingual glosses transliterate consistently: Spanish 'Nacor/Najor,' French 'Nahor,' German 'Nachor.'

gloss_terse: Nethinim: temple servants 'given' to assist the Levites in sanctuary duties, prominent in post-exilic texts.
gloss_readable: A masculine plural noun derived from the passive participle of natan ('to give'), designating a class of temple servants assigned to support the Levites in maintaining the sanctuary. They appear almost exclusively in the post-exilic books of Ezra, Nehemiah, and 1 Chronicles, where they are carefully distinguished from priests, Levites, and gatekeepers (Ezra 2:43-58; 7:7; Neh 7:46-60). Tradition ascribes their appointment to David (Ezra 8:20), and they resided on the Ophel hill near the temple (Neh 3:26; 11:21). Their separate listing among the returnees from Babylon underscores their recognized, if humble, role in Israel's worship. Spanish renders them as 'sirvientes del templo,' while German uses 'Tempeldiener,' both accurately conveying their servant function.

senses.1: A dedicated class of hereditary temple servants whose title, from the passive of natan ('to give'), marks them as persons formally 'given' to sacred service. They assisted the Levites in menial sanctuary tasks and are carefully enumerated among the exilic returnees (Ezra 2:43-58; Neh 7:46-60), distinguished from priests, Levites, and gatekeepers. They lived on the Ophel near the temple (Neh 3:26; 11:21). David is credited with their appointment (Ezra 8:20). Multilingual glosses consistently describe their servant role: Spanish 'sirvientes del templo,' German 'Tempeldiener,' French 'Nethiniens.'

gloss_terse: Succoth: 'booths,' a city in Transjordan linked to Jacob; also an exodus staging point in Egypt.
gloss_readable: A place name meaning 'booths' or 'shelters,' designating at least two biblical locations. The primary Succoth lies in the Jordan Valley east of the river, where Jacob built shelters for his livestock after parting from Esau (Gen 33:17). This city figures prominently in Gideon's pursuit of the Midianite kings, whose elders refused him bread and paid dearly for it (Judg 8:5-16). It also appears in the 'Valley of Succoth' that God parcels out in the psalms of confidence (Ps 60:6; 108:7) and near the bronze-casting site for Solomon's temple vessels (1 Kgs 7:46). A second Succoth marks the first stop after the Israelites departed Rameses in the exodus (Exod 12:37; 13:20; Num 33:5-6). The Septuagint renders the name as Sokcchoth, while Genesis offers the Greek equivalent Skenai ('tents').

senses.1: A place name meaning 'booths,' referring primarily to a Transjordanian city in the Jordan Valley where Jacob erected shelters for his flocks (Gen 33:17), and which features in Gideon's Midianite campaign (Judg 8:5-16), Solomon's bronze casting (1 Kgs 7:46), and the psalmic division of the land (Ps 60:6; 108:7). A second Succoth is the initial staging point of the exodus from Egypt (Exod 12:37; 13:20). The Septuagint renders the etymological sense with Skenai ('tents') in Genesis while transliterating elsewhere as Sokcchoth.

gloss_terse: Most High: an Aramaic divine epithet for God as supreme sovereign, used exclusively in Daniel.
gloss_readable: An Aramaic adjective in the emphatic state meaning 'highest' or 'most exalted,' serving as a title for God throughout the Aramaic sections of Daniel. It appears both with the noun for God, as 'the Most High God' (Dan 3:26; 5:18, 21), and independently as a divine title, 'the Most High' (Dan 4:14, 21, 22, 29, 31; 7:25). The term emphasizes God's absolute sovereignty over earthly kingdoms, a theme central to Nebuchadnezzar's humbling and restoration (Dan 4). Its ketiv-qere variation (written as illai, read as illaa) reflects typical Aramaic orthographic convention. The epithet parallels the Hebrew Elyon found in Genesis 14 and the Psalms, extending the same theology of divine supremacy into the Aramaic court narratives.

senses.1: An Aramaic divine epithet designating God as supreme ruler over all earthly and heavenly powers. Used in Daniel's court narratives both attributively ('the Most High God,' Dan 3:26; 5:18, 21) and as a standalone title ('the Most High,' Dan 4:14, 21, 29, 31; 7:25). The ketiv-qere alternation reflects standard Aramaic scribal convention. This title parallels Hebrew Elyon and underscores the book's central claim that God deposes and raises kings at will. Multilingual glosses capture the superlative force: Spanish 'Altisimo,' German 'der Hoechste.'

gloss_terse: Ammonite: a gentilic adjective for the people of Ammon, Israel's eastern Transjordanian neighbor.
gloss_readable: A gentilic noun and adjective identifying members of the nation of Ammon, a Transjordanian people descended from Lot's younger daughter (Gen 19:38). The term appears in singular, plural, and feminine forms across legal, narrative, and prophetic texts. Deuteronomy excludes the Ammonite from the assembly of the Lord (Deut 23:3; Neh 13:1). Nahash the Ammonite threatens Jabesh-gilead (1 Sam 11:1-2), and Solomon's foreign wives include Ammonite women, most notably Naamah, mother of Rehoboam (1 Kgs 14:21, 31; 11:1). In Nehemiah, Tobiah the Ammonite is a persistent antagonist to the rebuilding effort (Neh 2:10, 19; 3:35). Spanish 'amonita/amonitas,' French 'Ammonite/Ammonites,' and German 'Ammoniter' all directly transliterate the gentilic form.

senses.1: A gentilic designation for persons belonging to the nation of Ammon, east of the Jordan. The term functions both as adjective ('Ammonite women,' 1 Kgs 11:1; Neh 13:23) and substantive ('the Ammonite,' 1 Sam 11:1; Neh 2:10). Legal texts bar Ammonites from the Israelite assembly (Deut 23:3; Neh 13:1), while narrative texts feature individual Ammonites such as Nahash (1 Sam 11:1), Naamah (1 Kgs 14:21), and Tobiah (Neh 2:10). Multilingual glosses uniformly transliterate: Spanish 'amonita,' French 'Ammonite,' German 'Ammoniter.'
